title: Boyle's Law in Detail — Isotherms, Numericals and Limitations
notes: The first gas law in full: statement, graphs, molecular explanation, numericals and where it breaks — the pattern to reproduce for Charles' and Avogadro's laws.

At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure: V ∝ 1/P, i.e. PV = constant, or P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. Conditions: fixed mass, constant T, ideal behaviour (low P).
• P versus V: rectangular hyperbola (each temperature gives one hyperbola — an isotherm; higher T curves lie farther from the origin).
• P versus 1/V: straight line through the origin, slope = nRT.
• PV versus P: horizontal straight line for an ideal gas; real gases show a dip (attraction) then a rise (volume effect) — the first visible sign of non-ideality.

Halving the volume doubles the number density of molecules, so wall collisions per unit area per second double, doubling the pressure — the inverse relation is pure collision statistics at fixed average molecular speed (fixed T).
• V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂: 500 cm³ at 700 mm Hg → at 1400 mm Hg: 250 cm³.
• Density application: since m fixed, d ∝ P at constant T — a compressed gas is proportionally denser.
• Bubble problem: an air bubble rising from depth doubles its volume as pressure halves (plus water-column corrections with 10 m water ≈ 1 atm).
• Ideal-gas law: fails at high pressure (PV rises above nRT) and near liquefaction; gases with strong attraction (CO₂, SO₂, NH₃) deviate most; H₂ and He deviate least.
• Requires fixed mass and constant temperature — a temperature change during compression invalidates it.
• Cannot be extrapolated to the liquid state; below the critical temperature compression produces condensation, not further Boyle-law shrinkage.
confusion: ❌ PV = constant for any gas under any conditions. ✅ Only for fixed mass at constant temperature and ideal behaviour.
❌ Doubling pressure halves the temperature. ✅ Boyle's law holds T constant; the P–T relation is Gay-Lussac's law.
❌ The P–V graph is a straight line. ✅ It is a hyperbola; the straight line appears for P versus 1/V.

At constant T the product PV equals nRT for every ideal gas; its graph versus P is flat.
Real-gas Boyle plots dip below the ideal line at moderate pressure — evidence of intermolecular attraction.
examples: **Problem:** A diver's air bubble of 5 mL forms at 4 atm (depth ≈30 m). What volume at the surface (1 atm), ignoring temperature change? **Solution:** V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂ = 4 × 5/1 = 20 mL — a fourfold expansion, the classic Boyle's law safety example.

summary: Boyle's law, published by Robert Boyle in 1662, states that at constant temperature the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure, so V ∝ 1/P and PV = constant or P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. The P–V graph is a rectangular hyperbola, each temperature giving one isotherm, while P against 1/V is a straight line through the origin with slope nRT, and PV against P is horizontal for an ideal gas but dips and then rises for a real gas. Microscopically, halving the volume doubles the number density and so doubles the wall-collision rate and the pressure. The law fails at high pressure, near liquefaction, and for gases with strong attraction such as CO₂, SO₂ and NH₃.
importantConcepts: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ for a fixed mass at constant temperature and ideal behaviour
Isotherm — one rectangular hyperbola per temperature, with higher-temperature curves farther from the origin
P against 1/V as a straight line through the origin with slope nRT
PV against P horizontal for an ideal gas, but dipping then rising for a real gas
Molecular explanation: halving the volume doubles the number density and hence the wall-collision rate
Density consequence: at constant T with fixed mass, d ∝ P
importantStatements: Boyle published the law in 1662, the first quantitative gas law.
At constant temperature the product PV equals nRT for every ideal gas, so a PV-versus-P plot is flat.
Halving the volume doubles the pressure, so 500 cm³ at 700 mm Hg becomes 250 cm³ at 1400 mm Hg.
An air bubble of 5 mL formed at 4 atm expands to 20 mL at the surface where the pressure is 1 atm.
A rising air bubble doubles its volume as the surrounding pressure halves, with 10 m of water corresponding to about 1 atm.
Real gases deviate most at high pressure and near liquefaction; H₂ and He deviate least while CO₂, SO₂ and NH₃ deviate most.

keyPoints: State the two conditions — fixed mass and constant temperature — every time the law is quoted.
PV is constant only under those conditions; it changes when T or n changes.
The P–V graph is a hyperbola, not a straight line; the straight line appears for P against 1/V.
Draw the PV-versus-P horizontal line with the real-gas dip to show mastery beyond the ideal law.
Boyle's law cannot be extrapolated into the liquid state, where compression produces condensation instead.
specialNotes: A temperature change during compression invalidates the law, so an isotherm must be maintained throughout.
Below the critical temperature, compression produces condensation rather than further Boyle-law shrinkage, so the liquid state lies outside the law's scope.
The real-gas Boyle plot dips below the ideal line at moderate pressure, which is direct experimental evidence of intermolecular attraction.
Gases with strong attraction such as CO₂, SO₂ and NH₃ deviate most, while the small non-polar H₂ and He deviate least.
For a bubble rising through water, remember that 10 m of water column corresponds to about 1 atm.
examShortTricks: State the two conditions — fixed mass, constant temperature — every single time.
Cross-multiply rather than rearranging: V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂.
If the pressure doubles, the volume halves; if it quadruples, the volume quarters.
Sketch the PV-versus-P horizontal line with the real-gas dip to demonstrate the ideal and real cases together.
examNotes: Usually a 2–3 mark statement with a graph, often as the opening part of a gas-laws question.
A 2–3 mark numerical on P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ is very common, including diver and bubble problems.
Explaining the law through the kinetic theory earns the reasoning marks in a 5-mark question.
Limitations are asked as a short follow-up, with high pressure and liquefaction as the expected points.
